General Coverage Models: Structure, Monotonicity, and Shotgun Sequencing

Yitzchak Grunbaum    Eitan Yaakobi
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We study coverage processes in which each draw reveals a subset of [n][n], and the goal is to determine the expected number of draws until all items are seen at least once. A classical example is the Coupon Collector’s Problem, where each draw reveals exactly one item. Motivated by shotgun DNA sequencing, we introduce a model where each draw is a contiguous window of fixed length, in both cyclic and non-cyclic variants. We develop a unifying combinatorial tool that shifts the task of finding coverage time from probability, to a counting problem over families of subsets of [n][n] that together contain all items, enabling exact calculation. Using this result, we obtain exact expressions for the window models. We then leverage past results on a continuous analogue of the cyclic window model to analyze the asymptotic behavior of both models. We further study what we call uniform ℓ\ell-regular models, where every draw has size ℓ\ell and every item appears in the same number of admissible draws. We compare these to the batch sampling model, in which all ℓ\ell-subsets are drawn uniformly at random and present upper and lower bounds, which were also obtained independently by Berend and Sher. We conjecture, and prove for special cases, that this model maximizes the coverage time among all uniform ℓ\ell-regular models. Finally, we prove a universal upper bound on the entire class of uniform ℓ\ell-regular models, which illuminates the fact that many sampling models share the same leading asymptotic order, while potentially differing significantly in lower-order terms.

Index Terms:
DNA data storage, Shotgun sequencing, The coupon collector’s problem, Group drawings, Coverage problems.

I Introduction

Coverage problems refer to a class of problems in which there are [n][n] items to draw from, and on each draw a subset is obtained. The question of interest is finding the expected number of draws until all (or some of) the items are collected. One way to describe those problems more rigorously is by considering a hypergraph on [n][n], with {0,1,…,n−1}\{0,1,...,n-1\} being the vertices, and all admissible groups we can draw from constituting the hyperedges. Then, the question translates to finding the expected number of draws of hyperedges until all (or a subset of the) vertices are covered, where by being covered we mean that the vertex was contained in one of the drawn hyperedges.

Perhaps the most basic and well-known example to represent this family of problems is the Coupon Collector’s Problem. The coupon collector’s problem, introduced in early probability theory ([7, 8]), asks for the expected number of draws needed to collect all nn unique coupons under uniform sampling. In hypergraph language, it means that the hyperedges are singletons, making each i∈[n]i\in[n] have a degree of 1. The solution to this problem is n​HnnH_{n}, where HnH_{n} is the nnth harmonic number, which grows as n​log⁡nn\log n for large nn ([10, 9]). Extensions of this problem have considered non-uniform sampling or collecting subsets instead of single elements ([12, 13, 14, 15]).

Recent works have explored many connections between the coupon collector’s problem and DNA storage systems ([16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 5]). These include problems such as minimizing coverage depth, ensuring random access, and analyzing fragment overlap structures. In this paper, a connection between shotgun sequencing and the coupon collector’s problem is drawn. Shotgun sequencing is a powerful method in DNA sequencing, where long DNA molecules are fragmented into overlapping pieces that are sequenced and computationally assembled ([1, 2, 3]).

In recent years, shotgun sequencing principles have extended beyond biology into information storage, such as DNA storage systems ([4]). These applications motivate probabilistic models that quantify coverage requirements under structured sampling.

A central question in this setting is: how many fragments must be sampled to ensure full coverage of the original sequence? While practical sequencing involves additional considerations such as assembly heuristics and error correction, the probabilistic aspect of achieving complete coverage is a fundamental challenge with implications for both biology and information theory.

Motivated by the structure of shotgun sequencing, we consider a new model in which each observation corresponds to a consecutive window within a sequence. Unlike classical models where subsets are arbitrary, consecutive windows introduce strong dependencies that alter the dynamics of coverage. We consider both cyclic and non-cyclic models, and refer to them correspondingly the cyclic windows coverage problem and the windows coverage problem.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the definitions that are used throughout the paper, and states 4 problems, with two of them being the window models mentioned above (Problems 1 and 2), another problem is a continuous version of Problem 2 (Problem 3), and lastly a problem which is referred to as the batch coverage problem (Problem 4) which is the problem of drawing coupons in groups of the same size and any subset is equally likely to be sampled. Inspired by recent work that recasts expectations as combinatorial counts (e.g., [17]), in Section III we develop a compact, unifying tool that reduces the computation of expected coverage time to counting what we call recovery sets in a corresponding hypergraph, which are sets of hyperedges that together contain all vertices. Section IV utilizes this tool to solve Problem 1, and presents more compact solutions for special cases. Section V is the second to make us of this method, and solves Problem 2. Section VI makes a comparison between Problems 2 and 3, allowing to derive bounds and understand the asymptotic behavior of both Problems 1 and 2. Section VII shows lower and upper bounds for the batch coverage model, which were derived essentially at the same time as the independent result of [28]. It introduces a question regarding all coverage problems for which the corresponding hypergraph is uniform ℓ\ell-regular, i.e., all hyperedges are of the same size, and all vertices have the same degree, and suggests that a monotonicity property holds: Restricting the drawings to only a subset of the hyperedges, while keeping uniformity might accelerate coverage in expectation, with a proof provided for some cases, and a conjecture that this is always the case and that among all uniform regular models, the batch coverage model achieves the highest expected coverage time. In this sense, the batch model serves as a universal upper bound for the expected time to full coverage across all such models. Although a lack of formal proof, partial proofs and empirical evidence strongly supports the conjecture that the batch coverage model indeed forms the upper bound for all uniform regular models. Nevertheless, a provable universal upper bound is established, slightly above the batch model’s expectation, guaranteeing that all those coverage models remains within the same asymptotic scale. Lastly, Section VIII outlines the remaining questions and a few directions for future research.

The Windows Coverage Problem. Consider the process of drawing i.i.d. ω1,ω2,…\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\dots uniformly at random from 𝒲n,ℓ\mathcal{W}_{n,\ell}. The coverage time is the random variable defined as

Tn,ℓ=min⁡{t:⋃r=1tωr=[n]}.T_{n,\ell}\;=\;\min\Big\{t:\ \bigcup_{r=1}^{t}\omega_{r}=[n]\Big\}.

The problem is to determine the expected coverage time, denoted by 𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}].

Problem 4.

The Batch Coverage Problem. Fix nn and ℓ\ell. Consider the process of drawing subsets S1,S2,…S_{1},S_{2},\ldots, referred to as batches, of size |Si|=ℓ|S_{i}|=\ell uniformly from {S⊆[n]:|S|=ℓ}\{S\subseteq[n]:|S|=\ell\}. The coverage time is defined as

III A General Combinatorial Approach for
Solving Coverage Problems

Before we study the proposed coverage problems in this paper, we first seek to establish a general combinatorial approach which will be used in our analysis throughout the paper. This approach, motivated by the work of [17], produces a tool which converts the problem of calculating the expectation of the coverage time to a combinatorial problem in which the expectation can be expressed in a combinatorial fashion. While the motivation in [17] was to study the so-called random access problem in DNA-based storage systems, the approach can be extended in a more general form.

All coverage problems share a common structure in which the expected time to full coverage admits a single, model-independent expression that only depends on the number of recovery sets that will be defined next. Thus, the task of computing the expectation reduces to a combinatorial problem of counting recovery sets. First, we show a general framework to present coverage problems using hypergraphs.

Definition 1.

A hypergraph is a pair ℋ=(V,E)\mathcal{H}=(V,E) where

  • •

    VV is a finite set of vertices, and

  • •

    E⊆2VE\subseteq 2^{V} consists of non-empty subsets of VV, called hyperedges.

A hypergraph is said to be covering if ⋃e∈Ee=V\bigcup_{e\in E}e=V.

Definition 2.

Let Ω\Omega be a set of nn coverable objects, i.e., |Ω|=n|\Omega|=n. A coverage model is specified by a finite family of observable blocks 𝒜={A1,…,ANℋ}\mathcal{A}=\{A_{1},\dots,A_{N_{\mathcal{H}}}\}, where each Ai⊆ΩA_{i}\subseteq\Omega is the set of objects revealed by a single draw. Equivalently, the coverage model can be presented using a hypergraph

ℋ=(V,E),V=Ω,E=𝒜⊆2V,\mathcal{H}=(V,E),\qquad V=\Omega,\quad E=\mathcal{A}\subseteq 2^{V},

where the vertices are the objects and the hyperedges are the observable blocks. The hypergraph ℋ\mathcal{H} is assumed to be covering. On each round, an index Ir∈[Nℋ]I_{r}\in[N_{\mathcal{H}}] is uniformly and independently sampled, revealing the IrI_{r}-th hyperedge and collecting its vertices AIrA_{I_{r}}. The coverage time is defined to be

Tℋ=min⁡{t:⋃r=1tAIr=Ω}.T_{\mathcal{H}}\;=\;\min\Big\{t:\ \bigcup_{r=1}^{t}A_{I_{r}}\,=\,\Omega\Big\}.

A recovery set is a subset of the hyperedges ℛ⊆𝒜\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{A} such that ⋃ℰ∈ℛℰ=Ω\bigcup_{\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{E}=\Omega. The set of all recovery sets is defined as Rec⁡(𝒜):={ℛ⊆𝒜:ℛ​ is a recovery set}.\mathrm{Rec}(\mathcal{A}):=\big\{\,\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\ :\mathcal{R}\text{ is a recovery set}\}. Denote MℋM_{\mathcal{H}} as the maximal size of any non-recovery set, that is, Mℋ=max⁡{|ℛ|:ℛ∈2𝒜∖Rec⁡(𝒜)}M_{\mathcal{H}}=\max\Big\{\,|\mathcal{R}|\ :\mathcal{R}\in 2^{\mathcal{A}}\setminus\mathrm{Rec}(\mathcal{A})\}. And denote αℋ​(s)\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s) to be the number of ss-sized recovery sets. Explicitly αℋ​(s)=|{ℛ∈Rec⁡(𝒜):|ℛ|=s}|\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)=|\{\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{Rec}(\mathcal{A}):|\mathcal{R}|=s\}|. When the hypergraph is obvious from context, we omit the H subscript.

The following examples illustrate how a coverage problem can be presented by a hypergraph.

Example 5.

Classical Coupon Collector’s Problem. V=[n]V=[n], E={{i}:i∈V}E=\{\{i\}:i\in V\}, Nℋ=nN_{\mathcal{H}}=n. Each draw reveals a singleton; coverage means every vertex has been sampled.

For binary vectors u,v∈{0,1}du,v\in\{0,1\}^{d}, their Hamming distance is distH⁡(u,v)=|{i∈[d]:ui≠vi}|.\operatorname{dist}_{H}(u,v)=|\{\,i\in[d]:u_{i}\neq v_{i}\,\}|. For a binary vector v∈{0,1}dv\in\{0,1\}^{d} and radius t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, the Hamming ball of radius tt centered at vv is Bt​(v)={u∈{0,1}d:distH⁡(u,v)≤t}.B_{t}(v)=\{\,u\in\{0,1\}^{d}:\operatorname{dist}_{H}(u,v)\leq t\,\}.

Example 6.

Hamming Hypercube Coverage. Fix d,t∈ℕd,t\in\mathbb{N}. Let V={0,1}dV=\{0,1\}^{d} be the set of vertices of the dd-dimensional Hamming hypercube, so |V|=2d|V|=2^{d}. Let

E={Bt​(x):x∈V}E=\{\,B_{t}(x):x\in V\,\}

be the family of all Hamming balls of radius tt. Then Nℋ=|V|=2dN_{\mathcal{H}}=|V|=2^{d}. Each draw reveals a Hamming ball of radius tt; coverage means that every vertex lies in some revealed ball.

Theorem 1.

Given a hypergraph ℋ\mathcal{H},

𝔼⁡[Tℋ]=Nℋ​(HNℋ−HNℋ−Mℋ−1)−∑s=0Mℋαℋ​(s)(Nℋ−1s).\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}]=N_{\mathcal{H}}\big(H_{N_{\mathcal{H}}}-H_{N_{\mathcal{H}}-M_{\mathcal{H}}-1}\big)-\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\frac{\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)}{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}-1}{s}}.
Proof:

By the tail-sum formula, 𝔼⁡[Tℋ]=∑r≥1Pr⁡(Tℋ≥r).\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}]\;=\;\sum_{r\geq 1}\Pr\!\big(T_{\mathcal{H}}\geq r\big). Let μr\mu_{r} denote the number of distinct hyperedges revealed after rr rounds. By the law of total probability and since any set of size greater than MℋM_{\mathcal{H}} is a recovery set, Pr⁡(Tℋ≥r)=∑s=0MℋPr⁡(Tℋ≥r∣μr−1=s)​Pr⁡(μr−1=s).\Pr\!\big(T_{\mathcal{H}}\geq r\big)=\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\Pr\!\big(T_{\mathcal{H}}\geq r\mid\mu_{r-1}=s\big)\,\Pr\!\big(\mu_{r-1}=s\big). Conditioned on μr−1=s\mu_{r-1}=s, Pr⁡(Tℋ≥r∣μr−1=s)=1−αℋ​(s)(Nℋs),\Pr\!\big(T_{\mathcal{H}}\geq r\mid\mu_{r-1}=s\big)=1-\frac{\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)}{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}}{s}}, since αℋ​(s)\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s) counts the size-ss recovery sets among the (Nℋs)\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}}{s} many ss-subsets. Moreover, by the inclusion–exclusion principle,

Pr⁡(μr−1=s)=(Nℋs)​∑j=0s(sj)​(−1)j​(s−jNℋ)r−1.\Pr\!\big(\mu_{r-1}=s\big)=\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}}{s}\sum_{j=0}^{s}\binom{s}{j}(-1)^{j}\Big(\frac{s-j}{N_{\mathcal{H}}}\Big)^{r-1}.

Therefore,

𝔼⁡[Tℋ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}] =∑r≥1∑s=0Mℋ(1−αℋ​(s)(Nℋs))​(Nℋs)​∑j=0s(sj)​(−1)j​(s−jNℋ)r−1\displaystyle=\sum_{r\geq 1}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\Big(\hskip-1.07639pt1\hskip-1.07639pt-\hskip-1.07639pt\frac{\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)}{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}}{s}}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\Big)\hskip-1.07639pt\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}}{s}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\sum_{j=0}^{s}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\binom{s}{j}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt(-1)^{j}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\Big(\hskip-1.07639pt\frac{s-j}{N_{\mathcal{H}}}\hskip-1.07639pt\Big)^{\hskip-0.75346pt\hskip-0.75346pt\hskip-0.75346ptr-1}
=∑s=0Mℋ((Nℋs)−αℋ​(s))​∑j=0s(sj)​(−1)j​∑r≥0(s−jNℋ)r\displaystyle=\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\big(\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}}{s}-\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)\big)\sum_{j=0}^{s}\binom{s}{j}(-1)^{j}\sum_{r\geq 0}\Big(\frac{s-j}{N_{\mathcal{H}}}\Big)^{r}

𝔼⁡[Tℋ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}] =∑s=0Mℋ(Nℋs)−αℋ​(s)(Nℋ−1s)=∑s=0Mℋ(Nℋs)(Nℋ−1s)−∑s=0Mℋαℋ​(s)(Nℋ−1s)\displaystyle=\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\frac{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}}{s}-\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)}{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}-1}{s}}=\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\frac{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}}{s}}{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}-1}{s}}-\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\frac{\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)}{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}-1}{s}}
=Nℋ​∑s=0Mℋ1Nℋ−s−∑s=0Mℋαℋ​(s)(Nℋ−1s)\displaystyle=N_{\mathcal{H}}\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{H}}-s}-\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\frac{\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)}{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}-1}{s}}
=Nℋ​(HNℋ−HNℋ−Mℋ−1)−∑s=0Mℋαℋ​(s)(Nℋ−1s).\displaystyle=N_{\mathcal{H}}\big(H_{N_{\mathcal{H}}}-H_{N_{\mathcal{H}}-M_{\mathcal{H}}-1}\big)-\sum_{s=0}^{M_{\mathcal{H}}}\frac{\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s)}{\binom{N_{\mathcal{H}}-1}{s}}.

∎This approach reduces the task of determining the expected coverage time to computing MM and αℋ​(s)\alpha_{\mathcal{H}}(s). Once these are known, the expectation follows immediately from Theorem 1, turning the probabilistic question into a purely combinatorial calculation.

Theorem 1 is now used to compute the expectation in Examples 5 and 6, illustrating how straightforward this approach is in practice.

Example 5 (continued). Classical Coupon Collector’s Problem. There are no recovery sets of size s≤n−1s\leq n-1, i.e. α⁡(s)=0\alpha(s)=0 for s≤n−1s\leq n-1. Hence, by Theorem 1, the expected number of draws is n​HnnH_{n}.

Example 6 (continued). Hamming Hypercube Coverage. The maximum size of a non–recovery set is M=N−|Bt|= 2d−∑j=0t(dj),M\;=\;N-|B_{t}|\;=\;2^{d}-\sum_{j=0}^{t}\binom{d}{j}, since a vertex vv remains uncovered if and only if all balls containing vv are omitted. Hence, by Theorem 1, the expected number of draws is

2d​(H2d−H|Bt|−1)−∑s=0 2d−|Bt|α⁡(s)(2d−1s),2^{d}\big(H_{2^{d}}-H_{\,|B_{t}|-1}\big)\;-\;\sum_{s=0}^{\,2^{d}-|B_{t}|}\frac{\alpha(s)}{\binom{2^{d}-1}{s}},

where α⁡(s)\alpha(s) counts all size-ss collections of radius-tt balls whose union is the entire cube.

From here on, for every coverage model throughout the paper, we will refer to the possible attainable subsets of collectable items as the hyperedges of the graph of items interchangeably.

IV Problem 1: The Windows Coverage Model

In this section we solve Problem 1, the window coverage problem.

IV-A General Solution to The Windows Coverage Problem

Using the approach derived in Section III, Problem 1 can be formulated using hypergraphs as follows. Denote

ℋn,ℓ=(V,E),V=[n],E=𝒜=𝒲n,ℓ,\mathcal{H}_{n,\ell}=(V,E),\qquad V=[n],\qquad E=\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{W}_{n,\ell},

so it holds that N=|E|=nN=|E|=n and M=n−ℓM=n-\ell (omitting the coverage of the rightmost position admits the largest non recovery set). Let α⁡(s)\alpha(s) denote the number of size-ss recovery sets in 𝒲n,ℓ\mathcal{W}_{n,\ell}. Then, by Theorem 1 it holds that,

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]=(n−ℓ+1)​Hn−ℓ+1−∑s=0n−ℓα⁡(s)(n−ℓs).\;\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]=(n-\ell+1)\,H_{\,n-\ell+1}\;-\;\sum_{s=0}^{\,n-\ell}\frac{\alpha(s)}{\binom{\,n-\ell\,}{s}}.\; (IV.1)

The task then reduces to determining the values of α⁡(s)\alpha(s), yielding the following.

Lemma 1.

It holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]= (n−ℓ+1)​Hn−ℓ+1\displaystyle(n-\ell+1)H_{n-\ell+1}
−∑s=⌈nℓ⌉n−ℓ∑i=0⌊n−ℓ−s+1ℓ⌋(−1)i(s−1i)⋅(n−ℓ−i​ℓ−1s−2)(n−ℓs).\displaystyle-\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\sum_{s=\left\lceil\hskip-0.75346pt\hskip-0.75346pt\frac{n}{\ell}\right\rceil}^{n-\ell}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\sum_{i=0}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n-\ell-s+1}{\ell}\right\rfloor}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt(-1)^{i}\binom{s-1}{i}\hskip-1.07639pt\cdot\hskip-1.07639pt\frac{\binom{n-\ell-i\ell-1}{s-2}}{\binom{n-\ell}{s}}.
In particular,
𝔼⁡[Tn,2]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T_{n,2}]= (n−1)​Hn−1−∑s=⌈n2⌉n−2(s−1n−s−1)(n−2s).\displaystyle(n-1)\,H_{\,n-1}-\sum_{s=\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil}^{\,n-2}\frac{\binom{\,s-1\,}{\,n-s-1\,}}{\binom{\,n-2\,}{s}}.
Proof:

The possible start positions for any window are {0,1,…,n−ℓ}\{0,1,\dots,n-\ell\}. Any size-ss recovery set must include the extreme windows. Denote a recovery set ℛ\mathcal{R}, and denote its corresponding set of start positions in an increasing order

ℐℛ={x1=0<x2<⋯<xs=n−ℓ}.\mathcal{I_{R}}=\{x_{1}=0<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{s}=n-\ell\}.

Let the gaps be δi=xi+1−xi∈{1,…,ℓ}\delta_{i}=x_{i+1}-x_{i}\in\{1,\dots,\ell\} with ∑i=1s−1δi=n−ℓ\sum_{i=1}^{s-1}\delta_{i}=n-\ell, and set δi′=δi−1∈{0,…,ℓ−1}\delta_{i}^{\prime}=\delta_{i}-1\in\{0,\dots,\ell-1\}. Then

∑i=1s−1δi′=n−ℓ−s+1⏟telescopic.\sum_{i=1}^{s-1}\delta_{i}^{\prime}=\underbrace{n-\ell-s+1}_{\text{telescopic}}.

For each ℛ∈Rec⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{Rec}(\mathcal{A}), ℐℛ\mathcal{I_{R}} corresponds to a unique set of gaps bijectively. Hence, α⁡(s)\alpha(s) equals the coefficient of xn−ℓ−s+1x^{\,n-\ell-s+1} in the generating function (1+x+⋯+xℓ−1)s−1\big(1+x+\cdots+x^{\ell-1}\big)^{s-1}. Therefore, by a standard derivation, it can be shown that α⁡(s)\alpha(s)\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt =∑i=0min⁡(s−1,⌊n−ℓ−s+1ℓ⌋)(−1)i(s−1i)(n−ℓ−i​ℓ−1s−2).\text{ }=\sum_{i=0}^{\min\!\left(s-1,\;\left\lfloor\frac{n-\ell-s+1}{\ell}\right\rfloor\right)}(-1)^{i}\binom{s-1}{i}\binom{\,n-\ell-i\ell-1\,}{\,s-2\,}\;. Note that α⁡(s)=0\alpha(s)=0 unless ⌈nℓ⌉≤s\lceil\tfrac{n}{\ell}\rceil\leq s, and note that for ℓ=2\ell=2, we get a simpler expression since δi′∈{0,1}\delta_{i}^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}, and thus α⁡(s)=(s−1n−s−1)\;\alpha(s)=\binom{s-1}{\,n-s-1\,}\;. ∎

Lemma 1 fully solves Problem 1 and gives an exact expression for the coverage time. Further, for the general case (arbitrary ℓ\ell), algebraic manipulation yields a more informative closed form.

IV-B Large Windows

This section presents the expected coverage time for special regimes of ℓ\ell relative to nn.

Theorem 3.

For all integers n2≤ℓ<n\frac{n}{2}\leq\ell<n, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]=32​(n−ℓ+1).\;\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]\;=\;\tfrac{3}{2}\,\big(n-\ell+1\big).\;
Proof:

Write M=n−ℓ+1M=n-\ell+1 for the number of windows. When ℓ≥n/2\ell\geq n/2, the two extreme windows, winℓ​(0)=[0,ℓ−1]\mathrm{win}_{\ell}(0)=[0,\ell-1] and winℓ​(n−ℓ)=[n−ℓ,n−1]\mathrm{win}_{\ell}(n-\ell)=[n-\ell,n-1], already cover all positions (each endpoint 00 and n−1n{-}1 belongs to exactly one of them). Hence full coverage occurs if and only if both extreme windows have appeared. Draws are i.i.d. uniform over the MM windows. The waiting time to see either extreme window is geometric with success probability 2/M2/M, of expectation M/2M/2. After the first extreme window is seen, the waiting time to see the other extreme window is geometric with success probability 1/M1/M, of expectation MM. By linearity of expectation,

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]=M2+M=32​M=32​(n−ℓ+1).\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]\;=\;\frac{M}{2}+M\;=\;\tfrac{3}{2}\,M\;=\;\tfrac{3}{2}\,(n-\ell+1).

∎

Theorem 4.

For all integers n3≤ℓ<n2\frac{n}{3}\leq\ell<\tfrac{n}{2}, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]=32​(n−ℓ+1)+(n−ℓ+1)​6​n−10​ℓℓ⁡(ℓ+1)​(ℓ+2)​(ℓ+3).\;\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]=\tfrac{3}{2}\,\big(n-\ell+1\big)\;+\;\big(n-\ell+1\big)\,\tfrac{6n-10\ell}{\ell(\ell+1)(\ell+2)(\ell+3)}\;.
Proof:

We first observe that full coverage occurs if and only if both extreme windows were sampled and all n−2​ℓn-2\ell middle positions are covered. So only coverage of the middle n−2​ℓ+2n-2\ell+2 positions matters. We model the process using a three-layered Markov chain. States are denoted by SikS_{i}^{k}, where i∈{0,1,…,n−2​ℓ}i\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-2\ell\} counts the number of unseen middle positions, and k∈{0,1,2}k\in\{0,1,2\} indicates how many extreme windows have been observed. Note that the uncovered middle positions always appear continuously. For each state SikS_{i}^{k}, the number of windows that cover all ii uncovered middle positions is ℓ−i+1\ell-i+1, giving the transition probability Pr[Sik→S0k]=ℓ−i+1n−ℓ+1\Pr[S_{i}^{k}\rightarrow S_{0}^{k}]=\tfrac{\ell-i+1}{n-\ell+1}. For each 1≤j<i1\leq j<i, the number of windows covering exactly i−ji-j new middle positions is exactly 2, giving a transition probability Pr[Sik→Sjk]=2n−ℓ+1\Pr[S_{i}^{k}\rightarrow S_{j}^{k}]=\tfrac{2}{n-\ell+1}. The number of windows that reveal an uncovered extreme window is 2−k2-k, giving a transition probability Pr[Sik→Sik+1]=2−kn−ℓ+1\Pr[S_{i}^{k}\rightarrow S_{i}^{k+1}]=\tfrac{2-k}{n-\ell+1}. Since all probabilities sum to 11, the transition probability of no new covered positions is Pr[Sik→Sik]=n−2​ℓ−i+kn−ℓ+1\Pr[S_{i}^{k}\rightarrow S_{i}^{k}]=\tfrac{n-2\ell-i+k}{n-\ell+1}. We solve the markov chain in a bottom up, as can be demonstrated visually in Figure 5.

For k=2k=2, using the transition probabilities, we derive the following recursive relation, E[S_i^2 →S_0^2]=1+ n - 2ℓ- i + 2 n - ℓ+ 1 E[S_i^2 →S_0^2]+ 2 n - ℓ+ 1 ∑_j = 1^i - 1 E[S_j^2 →S_0^2], and hence E[S_i^2 →S_0^2] = n - ℓ+ 1 ℓ- 1 + i + 2 ℓ- 1 + i ∑_j = 1^i - 1 E[S_j^2 →S_0^2]. And it can be shown by induction that

E[Si2→S02]=n−ℓ+1ℓ+n−ℓ+1ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)(i−1).E[S_{i}^{2}\to S_{0}^{2}]=\tfrac{n-\ell+1}{\ell}+\frac{n-\ell+1}{\ell(\ell+1)}(i-1).

Similarly, for k=1k=1, it can be derived that

+2ℓ+1+i​((n−ℓ+1)+n−ℓ+1ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)+2​(n−ℓ+1)ℓ​(ℓ+1)​(ℓ+2)​(i−1))\displaystyle+\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\tfrac{2}{\ell\hskip-0.75346pt+\hskip-0.75346pt1\hskip-0.75346pt+\hskip-0.75346pti}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\left(\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\small(n\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt-\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\ell\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt+\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt1\hskip-0.96873pt)\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt+\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\tfrac{n-\ell+1}{\ell(\ell+1)}\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt+\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\tfrac{2(n-\ell+1)}{\ell(\ell+1)(\ell+2)}(i\hskip-0.96873pt-\hskip-0.96873pt1)\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\right)\hskip-1.07639pt

𝔼[Si0→S02]=3​(n−ℓ+1)2+2​(n−ℓ+1)ℓ​(ℓ+1)​(ℓ+2)+6​(n−ℓ+1)ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)​(ℓ+2)​(ℓ+3)(i−1).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[S_{i}^{0}\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\to\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639ptS_{0}^{2}]\hskip-1.07639pt=\hskip-1.07639pt\tfrac{3(n-\ell+1)}{2}\hskip-1.07639pt+\hskip-1.07639pt\tfrac{2(n-\ell+1)}{\ell(\ell+1)(\ell+2)}\hskip-1.07639pt+\hskip-1.07639pt\tfrac{6(n-\ell+1)}{\ell(\ell+1)(\ell+2)(\ell+3)}(i-1).

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]=3​(n−ℓ+1)2+2​(n−ℓ+1)ℓ​(ℓ+1)​(ℓ+2)+6​(n−ℓ+1)​(n−2​ℓ−1)ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)​(ℓ+2)​(ℓ+3).\hskip-1.07639pt\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]\hskip-1.07639pt=\hskip-1.07639pt\tfrac{3(n-\ell+1)}{2}\hskip-1.07639pt+\hskip-1.07639pt\tfrac{2(n-\ell+1)}{\ell(\ell+1)(\ell+2)}\hskip-1.07639pt+\hskip-1.07639pt\tfrac{6(n-\ell+1)(n-2\ell-1)}{\ell(\ell+1)(\ell+2)(\ell+3)}.

Rearranging terms yields the expression in the theorem. ∎Note that this result also gives the expected number of steps required for getting from any i∈[n]i\in[n] uncovered positions, to jj.

After analyzing two specific cases representing the scenarios of large windows (ℓ≥n3\ell\geq\tfrac{n}{3}), lastly an analysis of a more general result is given in the next theorem.

Theorem 5.

For any ℓ≥nc\ell\geq\frac{n}{c} with a constant c>1c>1, it holds that

≤(a)​(c−2)​∑s=2n−2​ℓ+1sc−2⋅(n−2​ℓ−1s−2)(n−ℓs)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{\leq}(c-2)\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\hskip-1.07639pt\sum_{s=2}^{n-2\ell+1}s^{c-2}\cdot\tfrac{\binom{n-2\ell-1}{s-2}}{\binom{n-\ell}{s}}

V Problem 2: The Cyclic Windows Model

This section analyses Problem 2, the cyclic version of the windows coverage problem. First, a general solution is being presented. By applying Section III’s approach, we get that in the cyclic case, the hypergraph is

ℋn,ℓ↻=(V,E),V=[n],E=𝒜=𝒲n,ℓ↻.\mathcal{H}^{\circlearrowright}_{n,\ell}=(V,E),\qquad V=[n],\qquad E=\mathcal{A}=\ \mathcal{W}_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}.

As in Problem 1, α↻​(s)=0\alpha^{\circlearrowright}(s)=0 unless s≥⌈nℓ⌉s\geq\lceil\frac{n}{\ell}\rceil. Therefore, by Theorem 1,

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]=n⁡(Hn−Hℓ−1)−∑s=⌈nℓ⌉n−ℓα↻​(s)(n−1s).\mathbb{E}\!\big[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}\big]=n\big(H_{n}-H_{\ell-1}\big)-\sum_{s=\lceil\frac{n}{\ell}\rceil}^{\,n-\ell}\frac{\alpha^{\circlearrowright}(s)}{\binom{n-1}{s}}. (V.1)

In the same manner, the task reduces to determining α↻​(s)\alpha^{\circlearrowright}(s), yielding the following.

For all integers n>ℓ≥1n>\ell\geq 1, it holds that

Let w∗={n−1,0}w^{\ast}=\{n{-}1,0\} be the wrap–around window. We split according to whether w∗∈ℛw^{\ast}\in\mathcal{R}. In case w∗∉ℛw^{\ast}\notin\mathcal{R}, the problem is exactly as in Problem 1, hence we have (s−1n−s−1)\binom{s-1}{\,n-s-1\,} recovery sets not containing w∗w^{*}. In the case where w∗∈ℛw^{\ast}\in\mathcal{R}, {1,2,…,n−2}\{1,2,\dots,n-2\} must be covered using s−1s-1 windows from the remaining n−1n-1 edges {0,1},{1,2},…,{n−2,n−1}\{0,1\},\{1,2\},\dots,\{n-2,n-1\}. n−s,n−s−1,n−s−1,n−s−2.n-s,\quad n-s-1,\quad n-s-1,\quad n-s-2.

We now move on to the general case. A size-ss recovery set is specified by its ss start indices on the circle. Let β↻​(s)\beta^{\circlearrowright}(s) be the number of solutions, which is the number of cyclic recovery sets that contain 00. β↻​(s)=[xn−s]​(1+x+⋯+xℓ−1)s=∑j=0⌊n−sℓ⌋(−1)j​(sj)​(n−ℓ​j−1s−1).\displaystyle\beta^{\circlearrowright}(s)\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt=\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\big[x^{\,n\hskip-0.67812pt-\hskip-0.67812pts}\big]\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt(1\hskip-0.96873pt+\hskip-0.96873ptx\hskip-0.96873pt+\hskip-0.96873pt\cdots\hskip-0.96873pt+\hskip-0.96873ptx^{\ell\hskip-0.67812pt-\hskip-0.67812pt1}\hskip-0.96873pt)^{s}\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt=\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\sum_{j\hskip-0.67812pt=\hskip-0.67812pt0}^{\left\lfloor\tfrac{n\hskip-0.67812pt-\hskip-0.67812pts}{\ell}\right\rfloor}\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt(-1)^{j}\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\binom{s}{j}\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt\binom{\,n\hskip-0.96873pt-\hskip-0.96873pt\ell j\hskip-0.96873pt-\hskip-0.96873pt1\,}{\,s\hskip-0.96873pt-\hskip-0.96873pt1\,}\hskip-0.96873pt\hskip-0.96873pt.

To compute the number of recovery sets, a method similar to the one in the proof of Burnside’s Lemma for finite groups ([21]) is being used. In Section VII a monotonicity property is presented, regarding a family of sub models that Problem 2 induces and their multi-dimensional extensions.

VI Deriving Results and Bounds from Problem 3, The Continuous Circle

Problems 2 and 3 share a common structure. In both problems, arcs on a circle are being sampled until full coverage of the circumference. The two models can be compared and it is now shown that the discrete model has an expected number of samples that is at most the expected number in the continuous model.

Lemma 2.

For all 1≤ℓ≤n1\leq\ell\leq n, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]≤𝔼⁡[𝒯ℓn].\mathbb{E}\!\big[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}\big]\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{T}_{\frac{\ell}{n}}].
Proof:

The idea is that Tn,ℓT_{n,\ell}’s distribution can be created via 𝒯ℓn\mathcal{T}_{\frac{\ell}{n}}’s distribution, and it can be shown that for every sampled set of arcs that cover the circle, the corresponding created windows, cover the length-nn circle, thus showing a stochastic dominance of 𝒯ℓn\mathcal{T}_{\frac{\ell}{n}} over Tn,ℓT_{n,\ell}.

Let Ci∼Unif[0,1)C_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1), and define Di=⌊n​Ci⌋∈{0,1,…,n−1}.D_{i}=\lfloor nC_{i}\rfloor\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}. We interpret DiD_{i} as the starting index of a cyclic window of length ℓ\ell, i.e.,

winℓ​(Di)={Di,Di+1,…,Di+ℓ−1}(modn).\mathrm{win}_{\ell}(D_{i})=\{D_{i},D_{i}+1,\dots,D_{i}+\ell-1\}\pmod{n}.

Thus {Di}\{D_{i}\} is uniformly distributed over all nn possible window starts. Suppose the continuous arcs {[Cj,Cj+a)(mod1)}\{[C_{j},C_{j}+a)\pmod{1}\}, with a=ℓ/na=\ell/n already, cover the entire circle. Then for every index i∈{0,1,…,n−1}i\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}, the point xi=i/nx_{i}=i/n must lie inside some arc [Cr,Cr+a)[C_{r},C_{r}+a). Writing Dr=⌊n​Cr⌋D_{r}=\lfloor nC_{r}\rfloor, this immediately implies i∈winℓ​(Dr)i\in\mathrm{win}_{\ell}(D_{r}). Hence full coverage in the continuous model implies full coverage in the cyclic-discrete model.

∎

This upper bound helps concluding the asymptotic behavior of Problem 2.

Corollary 1.

For ℓ=o⁡(n)\ell=o(n), it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]≈nℓ​log⁡(nℓ).\mathbb{E}\!\big[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}\big]\approx\tfrac{n}{\ell}\log{\big(\tfrac{n}{\ell}\big)}.
Proof:

As mentioned in Section II, it was shown that 𝔼⁡[𝒯a]≈1a​log⁡(1a)​, as ​a→0.\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{T}_{a}]\approx\frac{1}{a}\,\log\!\Big(\frac{1}{a}\Big)\text{, as }a\rightarrow 0. According to this and Lemma 2, choosing a=ℓna=\frac{\ell}{n}, concludes that for ℓ=o⁡(n)\ell=o(n), 𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]≲nℓ​log⁡(nℓ).\mathbb{E}\!\big[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}\big]\lesssim\frac{n}{\ell}\,\log\!\Big(\frac{n}{\ell}\Big). Let m=⌊nℓ⌋m=\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor and take representatives S={0,ℓ,2​ℓ,…,(m−1)​ℓ}.S=\{0,\ell,2\ell,\dots,(m-1)\ell\}. Any length-ℓ\ell cyclic window covers only one element of SS, and for each i∈Si\in S the hit probability per draw is ℓn\frac{\ell}{n}. Thus the problem of covering SS reduces to the coupon collector’s problem ([7, 8, 9, 10, 11]) with ⌊nℓ⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor coupons. Therefore, 𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]≥⌊nℓ⌋​H⌊nℓ⌋≳nℓ​log⁡(nℓ).\mathbb{E}\!\big[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}\big]\ \geq\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor\,H_{\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor}\ \gtrsim\ \frac{n}{\ell}\,\log{\big(\frac{n}{\ell}\big)}. ∎Corollary 1 shows the intuitive observation that as nn grows and ℓ=o⁡(n)\ell=o(n), the discrete cyclic model shares the same leading asymptotic as the continuous circle covering problem. Now similarly to Section IV, the general asymptotic regime where ℓ=Ω⁡(n)\ell=\Omega(n) is examined, completing the asymptotic analysis of 𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}] for any ℓ≤n\ell\leq n.

Corollary 2.

Fix a constant c≥2c\geq 2. For nc≤ℓ<nc−1\frac{n}{c}\leq\ell\ <\frac{n}{c-1}, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]=O⁡(1).\mathbb{E}\!\big[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}\big]=O(1).

Furthermore, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]≤𝔼⁡[𝒯ℓ/n]≤𝔼⁡[𝒯1/c]≤1+c2.\mathbb{E}\!\big[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}\big]\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}\!\big[\mathcal{T}_{\ell/n}\big]\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}\!\big[\mathcal{T}_{1/c}\big]\leq 1+c^{2}.
Proof:

By Lemma 2 (Section VI), 𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻]≤𝔼⁡[𝒯a]\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}]\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{T}_{a}] with a=ℓna=\frac{\ell}{n}. If ℓ≥nc\ell\geq\frac{n}{c} then a≥1ca\geq\frac{1}{c}, and since covering gets easier as aa increases, 𝔼⁡[𝒯a]≤𝔼⁡[𝒯1/c]\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{T}_{a}]\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{T}_{1/c}]. Moreover, for tt samples of arcs, full coverage not occurs if and only if for every arc, the next one is at distance more than aa from it (which happens with probability 1−a1-a). By a union bound, the probability that this happens for all tt samples is at most t​(1−a)t−1t(1-a)^{t-1}. Hence,

𝔼⁡[Ta]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T_{a}]= ∑t=0∞Pr[Ta>t]=1+∑t=1∞Pr[Ta>t]\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\Pr[T_{a}>t]=1+\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\Pr[T_{a}>t]\;
≤\displaystyle\leq  1+∑t=1∞t​(1−a)t−1=1+1a2≤ 1+c2,\displaystyle\;1+\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}t(1-a)^{t-1}=1+\frac{1}{a^{2}}\;\leq\;1+c^{2},

showing that the bound depends purely on the ratio between nn and ℓ\ell. ∎

Going back to Problem 1, in order to analyze the asymptotic behavior of the expectation in this problem, we bound it from both sides, which yields the next result.

Theorem 7.

For ℓ=ω⁡(log⁡(n))\ell=\omega(\log(n)), it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]=32​(n−ℓ+1)​(1+o⁡(1)),\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]\;=\;\frac{3}{2}\,(n-\ell+1)\,\big(1+o(1)\big),

and for ℓ=o⁡(log⁡n)\ell=o(\log n), it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]=nℓ​log⁡(nℓ)​(1+o⁡(1)).\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]\;=\;\frac{n}{\ell}\,\log\!\Big(\frac{n}{\ell}\Big)\,\big(1+o(1)\big).
Proof:

The coverage expectation is at most the sum of expectations of covering the extremes [0,ℓ−1]∪[n−ℓ,n−1][0,\ell-1]\cup[n-\ell,n-1], and the complimentary middle regime [ℓ,n−ℓ−1][\ell,\,n-\ell-1] seperately. Roughly speaking, 𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]≤𝔼⁡[cover extremes]+𝔼⁡[cover middle].\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]\leq\mathbb{E}[\text{cover extremes}]+\mathbb{E}[\text{cover middle}]. As shown in Theorem 3, 𝔼⁡[cover extremes]=32​(n−ℓ+1).\mathbb{E}[\text{cover extremes}]\;=\;\tfrac{3}{2}\,(n-\ell+1). Covering only the middle is no harder than covering a full cyclic instance with n−ℓ+1n-\ell+1 positions and window length ℓ\ell, with a probability for each position to be covered that is identical in both cases, being ℓn−ℓ+1\tfrac{\ell}{n-\ell+1}. Therefore, 𝔼⁡[cover middle]≤𝔼⁡[Tn−ℓ+1,ℓ↻]≤𝔼⁡[𝒯a]​, with ​a=ℓn−ℓ+1\mathbb{E}[\text{cover middle}]\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\!\big[{T_{n-\ell+1,\ell}^{\circlearrowright}}\big]\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{a}\big]\text{, with }a=\frac{\ell}{n-\ell+1}, where the last inequality follows from Lemma 2. In addition, as mentioned in Section II, from [23, 24], 𝔼⁡[𝒯ℓn−ℓ+1]≈n−ℓ+1ℓ​log⁡(n−ℓ+1ℓ)≈nℓ​log⁡(nℓ)\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{T}_{\frac{\ell}{n-\ell+1}}]\approx\frac{n-\ell+1}{\ell}\log(\frac{n-\ell+1}{\ell})\approx\frac{n}{\ell}\log(\frac{n}{\ell}). Hence, the coverage time satisfies 𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]≲32​(n−ℓ+1)+nℓ​log⁡(nℓ)\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]\lesssim\tfrac{3}{2}\,(n-\ell+1)+\frac{n}{\ell}\log(\frac{n}{\ell}).

Additionally, the coverage time is at least as big as the coverage time to cover the extremes 32​(n−ℓ+1)\frac{3}{2}(n-\ell+1), and it is at least as big as the time to cover the representative points set S={ℓ−1,2​ℓ−1,3​ℓ−1,…​⌊n−ℓ+1ℓ⌋​ℓ−1}S=\{\ell-1,2\ell-1,3\ell-1,\dots\,\lfloor\frac{n-\ell+1}{\ell}\rfloor\ell-1\}. Each window covers only one representative point from SS, with probability ℓn−ℓ+1\frac{\ell}{n-\ell+1}, therefore, The problem reduces to the coupon collector’s problem ([7, 8, 9, 10, 11]) with ⌊n−ℓ+1ℓ⌋\lfloor\frac{n-\ell+1}{\ell}\rfloor coupons. Hence, 𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ]≥⌊n−ℓ+1ℓ⌋​H⌊n−ℓ+1ℓ⌋.\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]\ \geq\lfloor\tfrac{n-\ell+1}{\ell}\rfloor H_{\lfloor\tfrac{n-\ell+1}{\ell}\rfloor}. This gives the explicit bounds, max⁡{32​(n−ℓ+1),⌊n−ℓ+1ℓ⌋​H⌊n−ℓ+1ℓ⌋}≤𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ].\max\big\{\tfrac{3}{2}(n-\ell+1),\lfloor\tfrac{n-\ell+1}{\ell}\rfloor H_{\lfloor\frac{n-\ell+1}{\ell}\rfloor}\big\}\leq\mathbb{E}[T_{n,\ell}]. Therefore, by a simple analysis we get that for ℓ=ω⁡(log⁡(n))\ell=\omega(\log(n)) the linear term dominates, and for ℓ=o⁡(log⁡(n))\ell=o(\log(n)) the coupon collector term dominates, which makes the expectation asymptotically the same as in the cyclic case. ∎

Observation 1.

From Theorem 7, we observe that log⁡n\log n acts as a threshold on the expectation in the following way. Below it, the task is essentially “find all middle positions”, mirroring the cyclic behavior. Above it, the problem becomes essentially retrieving the two extremes.

VII The Batch Sampling Model and
Coverage Monotonicity

Problems 1, 2 and 4 ask for the time to cover nn items. Each model can be represented as hypergraph on [n][n] as mentioned and described in detail in Section III, with the collectable subsets of [n][n] being the hyperedges of the corresponding Problem’s hypergraph. In Problems 2 and 4, each item has the same degree (uniformity), each hyperedge has size ℓ\ell (regularity) and the set of hyperedges is non-empty. We call any hypergraph on [n][n] that satisfies those three conditions a uniform ℓ\ell-regular hypergraph on [n][n], or in short, a uniform ℓ\ell-regular model. Denote the class of all uniform ℓ\ell-regular hypergraphs on [n][n] as 𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}. For example, 𝒰n,1\mathcal{U}_{n,1} consists of only one hypergraph denoted by ℋn,1\mathcal{H}_{n,1} which is the hypergraph corresponding to the classical coupon collector’s problem, having 𝔼⁡[Tℋn,1]=n​Hn\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}_{n,1}}]=nH_{n}. Note that for any ℋ∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, the set of hyperedges is a subset of all possible hyperedges admissable in Problem 4 denoted as ([n]ℓ)\binom{[n]}{\ell}. Denote the hypergraph of Problem 4 as ℋ([n]ℓ)\mathcal{H}_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}. Note that Tℋ([n]ℓ)T_{\mathcal{H}_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}} is the same as the random variable in Problem 4, T([n]ℓ)T_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}, and will be referred to as such from now on.

In this section a natural question is suggested. Given ℋ1,ℋ2∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{H}_{1},\mathcal{H}_{2}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, with the corresponding sets of hyperedges ℱ1,ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2}, does it holds that if ℱ1⊆ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{2}, or even if |ℱ1|≤|ℱ2||\mathcal{F}_{1}|\leq|\mathcal{F}_{2}|, then 𝔼⁡[Tℋ1]≤𝔼⁡[Tℋ2]\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]\leq\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}_{2}}]? If so, ℋ([n]ℓ)\mathcal{H}_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}} with T([n]ℓ)T_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}} would have the highest expectation among 𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, and any model with nℓ\frac{n}{\ell} disjoint subsets would admit the lowest expectation. That is, for any ℋ∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, ⌊nℓ⌋​H⌊nℓ⌋≤𝔼⁡[Tℋ]≤𝔼⁡[T([n]ℓ)]\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor H_{\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor}\leq\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}]\leq\mathbb{E}[T_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}], providing universal upper and lower bounds on the expectation for the entire class.

As mentioned in Section II, combinatorial solutions for Problem 4 and the generalization, given A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n] with |A|=m|A|=m, and Zk​(A)Z_{k}(A) being the number of draws needed to see at least k≤mk\leq m distinct elements of AA, exact formulas were obtained. While exact, those expressions are numerically delicate for large parameters due to large binomial coefficients and cancellations, and is hard to compute in a regular calculator. The next results gives tight lower and upper bounds on the expectation of this problem, and furthermore for any generalization, as explained below.

While finalizing this paper, it was noticed that a very recent and concurrent work ([28]) independently presented a similar proof to the one presented here. We wish to acknowledge their contribution and give due credit. Nevertheless, the proof is included here, as we believe it serves a broader purpose, demonstrating that the same reasoning naturally extends to generalized versions of the coupon collector’s problem, including problems such as the double dixie cup and other variants. We also think and hope that the intuition in this proof can be applied in other coverage problems.

Theorem 8.

For any 1≤ℓ<n1\leq\ell<n and 1≤k≤m≤n1\leq k\leq m\leq n and A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n] with |A|=m|A|=m, it holds that

Hm−Hm−kHn−Hn−ℓ≤𝔼⁡[Zk​(A)]≤Hm−Hm−k−1nHn−Hn−ℓ+1.\frac{H_{m}-H_{m-k}}{\,H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}\,}\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}[Z_{k}(A)]\;\leq\;\frac{H_{m}-H_{m-k}-\frac{1}{n}}{\,H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}\,}+1.
Proof:

Fix A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n] with |A|=m≤n|A|=m\leq n and k≤mk\leq m. Let YY be the stopping time of the classical coupon collector’s problem with single coupon per draw, when kk items of AA were obtained. Since each new coupon from AA is obtained with probability m−jn\frac{m-j}{n}, after jj distinct ones have already been seen, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Y]=∑j=0k−1nm−j=n⁡(Hm−Hm−k).\mathbb{E}[Y]=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{n}{m-j}=n\bigl(H_{m}-H_{m-k}\bigr).

Let X:=Zk​(A)X:=Z_{k}(A) be the number of ℓ\ell-subset draws until the same coverage. From a single-coupon run i1,i2,…,iYi_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{Y}, form consecutive blocks by cutting as soon as the block contains ℓ\ell distinct coupon labels (within the block). Then, it is possible to partition i1,i2,…,iYi_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{Y} as follows.

i1,…,iY=\displaystyle i_{1},\ldots,i_{Y}=\ i1,…,iℓ+Z1⏟ℓ+Z1,iℓ+Z1+1,…,i2​ℓ+Z1+Z2⏟ℓ+Z2,…,\displaystyle\underbrace{i_{1},\ldots,i_{\ell+Z_{1}}}_{\ell+Z_{1}}\;,\;\underbrace{i_{\ell+Z_{1}+1},\ldots,i_{2\ell+Z_{1}+Z_{2}}}_{\ell+Z_{2}}\;,\;\ldots\;,
i(X−2)​ℓ+∑j=1X−2Zj+1,…,i(X−1)​ℓ+∑j=1X−1Zj⏟ℓ+ZX−1,\displaystyle\underbrace{i_{(X-2)\ell+\sum_{j=1}^{X-2}Z_{j}+1},\ldots,i_{(X-1)\ell+\sum_{j=1}^{X-1}Z_{j}}}_{\ell+Z_{X-1}}\;,\;
i(X−1)​ℓ+∑j=1X−1Zj+1,…,iY⏟partial block.\displaystyle\underbrace{i_{(X-1)\ell+\sum_{j=1}^{X-1}Z_{j}+1},\ldots,i_{Y}}_{\text{partial block}}\,.

The jj-th block then has length Lj=ℓ+ZjL_{j}=\ell+Z_{j}, where Zj≥0Z_{j}\geq 0 (wasted repeats inside the block). The expected number of draws until ℓ\ell distinct items were drawn is

𝔼⁡[Lj]=∑k=1ℓnn−k+1=n⁡(Hn−Hn−ℓ).\mathbb{E}[L_{j}]=\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}\tfrac{n}{n-k+1}=n(H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}).

Since Zj=Lj−ℓZ_{j}=L_{j}-\ell, we get

𝔼⁡[Zj]=𝔼⁡[Lj]−ℓ=n⁡(Hn−Hn−ℓ)−ℓ.\mathbb{E}[Z_{j}]=\mathbb{E}[L_{j}]-\ell=n\!\left(H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}\right)-\ell.

To derive the bounds, consider the following. After X−1X-1 blocks, the coverage process was almost finished, and the last draws until full coverage does not necessarily make a full block. Let D≥1D\geq 1 be the extra draws needed to reach full coverage after X−1X-1 blocks were drawn (by definition, X−1X-1 draws had not yet covered all items and at most one block is required to complete coverage). Then

Y=∑i=1X−1(ℓ+Zi)+D.Y\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{X-1}(\ell+Z_{i})\;+\;D.

Taking expectations gives

n⁡(Hm−Hm−k)−𝔼⁡[D]=ℓ​𝔼​[X−1]+𝔼⁡[X−1]​𝔼​[Z],n\big(H_{m}-H_{m-k}\big)-\mathbb{E}[D]\;=\;\ell\,\mathbb{E}[X-1]\;+\;\mathbb{E}[X-1]\mathbb{E}[Z],

which yields

𝔼⁡[X]=1+Hm−Hm−k−𝔼⁡[D]nHn−Hn−ℓ.\mathbb{E}[X]=1+\frac{H_{m}\hskip-1.07639pt-\hskip-1.07639ptH_{m-k}\hskip-1.07639pt-\hskip-1.07639pt\frac{\mathbb{E}[D]}{n}}{H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}}. (VII.1)

By the definition of DD, and since in the last DD draws the number of different collected items is at most ℓ\ell, it holds that 1≤𝔼⁡[D]≤𝔼⁡[Lj]1\leq\mathbb{E}[D]\leq\mathbb{E}[L_{j}]. Therefore, by substituting into Equation VII.1 we get the final bounds

Hm−Hm−kHn−Hn−ℓ≤𝔼⁡[X]≤1+Hm−Hm−k−1nHn−Hn−ℓ.\frac{H_{m}\hskip-1.07639pt-\hskip-1.07639ptH_{m-k}}{H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}}\leq\mathbb{E}[X]\leq 1\hskip-1.07639pt+\hskip-1.07639pt\frac{H_{m}\hskip-1.07639pt-\hskip-1.07639ptH_{m-k}\hskip-1.07639pt-\hskip-1.07639pt\frac{1}{n}}{H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}}.

∎Using Theorem 8, tight lower and upper bounds for Problem 4 are obtained. The special case of A=[n]A=[n], and k=nk=n, yields that for any 1≤ℓ≤n1\leq\ell\leq n,

HnHn−Hn−ℓ≤𝔼⁡[T([n]ℓ)]≤Hn−1Hn−Hn−ℓ+1,\frac{H_{n}}{\,H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}\,}\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}[T_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}]\;\leq\;\frac{H_{n-1}}{\,H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}\,}+1,

which coincides with the result of [28].

Next, more powerful statement is presented, explaining how Theorem 8 can be extended. We define the term coverage task as getting a collection that satisfies some requirement. The coupons collector’s problem has a coverage task that requires to obtain each coupon at least once. Another coverage task can be to obtain any coupon twice, as in the double dixie cups problem ([29]), or maybe to either get each one twice, or to get half of the coupons three time. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a coverage task. We can consider both ℋn,1\mathcal{H}_{n,1} and ℋ([n]ℓ)\mathcal{H}_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}} to be the hypergraphs from which hyperedges are being sampled, and we can ask about the relation of expected number of steps to complete 𝒞\mathcal{C} in both models. Denote Qn,1𝒞Q^{\mathcal{C}}_{{n,1}} as the number of hyperedges drawn from ℋn,1\mathcal{H}_{n,1} until completing 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and denote Qn,ℓ𝒞Q^{\mathcal{C}}_{{n,\ell}} as the number of draws until completing 𝒞\mathcal{C} drawing from ℋ([n]ℓ)\mathcal{H}_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}.

Theorem 9.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be any coverage task. It holds that

𝔼⁡[Qn,1𝒞]n⁡(Hn−Hn−ℓ)≤𝔼⁡[Qn,ℓ𝒞]≤𝔼⁡[Qn,1𝒞]−1nn⁡(Hn−Hn−ℓ)+1,\frac{\mathbb{E}[Q^{\mathcal{C}}_{n,1}]}{\,n\!\left(H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}\right)}\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}[Q^{\mathcal{C}}_{n,\ell}]\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbb{E}[Q^{\mathcal{C}}_{n,1}]-\frac{1}{n}}{\,n\!\left(H_{n}-H_{n-\ell}\right)}+1,
Proof:

The claim follows directly from the argument in the proof of Theorem 8, substituting X=Qn,ℓ𝒞X=Q_{n,\ell}^{\mathcal{C}} and Y=Qn,1𝒞Y=Q_{n,1}^{\mathcal{C}}. ∎This shows that any coverage task inherits the same normalization factor that governs the transition from using the single-coupon draws of ℋn,1\mathcal{H}_{n,1} to the ℓ\ell-subset draws of ℋ([n]ℓ)\mathcal{H}_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}.

One general framework that encompasses a broad family of coupon collector’s problem coverage tasks can be formulated as follows. Let

𝒗=(v1,v2,…,vn)∈ℕn{\boldsymbol{v}}=(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n}

be a demand vector, where viv_{i} specifies the required number of times item ii must be collected. We let Qn,1𝒗Q_{n,1}^{\boldsymbol{v}} denote the number of draws ℋn,1\mathcal{H}_{n,1}’s hyperedges required for obtaining each i∈[n]i\in[n] at least viv_{i} times, and Qn,ℓ𝒗Q_{n,\ell}^{\boldsymbol{v}} as number the of ℋ([n]ℓ)\mathcal{H}_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}’s hyperedges needed to complete the same task.

The double dixie cup problem mentioned above is a classical special case, obtained by setting a constant mm, and taking 𝒗=(m,m,…,m){\boldsymbol{v}}=(m,m,\ldots,m). In this setting ([29]) it is known that

𝔼⁡[Qn,1𝒗]=n⁡(log⁡n+(m−1)​log⁡log⁡n+γ+o⁡(1)).\mathbb{E}[Q_{n,1}^{\boldsymbol{v}}]=n\Bigl(\log n+(m-1)\log\log n+\gamma+o(1)\Bigr).

By Theorem 9, it is obtained that

𝔼⁡[Qn,ℓ𝒗]≥n⁡(log⁡n+(m−1)​log⁡log⁡n+γ+o⁡(1))n⁡(Hn−Hn−ℓ),\mathbb{E}[Q_{n,\ell}^{\boldsymbol{v}}]\geq\frac{n\Bigl(\log n+(m-1)\log\log n+\gamma+o(1)\Bigr)}{n(H_{n}-H_{n-\ell})},

and

𝔼⁡[Qn,ℓ𝒗]≤n⁡(log⁡n+(m−1)​log⁡log⁡n+γ+o⁡(1))−1nn⁡(Hn−Hn−ℓ)+1.\mathbb{E}[Q_{n,\ell}^{\boldsymbol{v}}]\leq\frac{n\Bigl(\log n+(m-1)\log\log n+\gamma+o(1)\Bigr)-\frac{1}{n}}{n(H_{n}-H_{n-\ell})}+1.

Note that the gap between the lower and upper bounds is at most 1, making the bounds tight.

Addressing the monotonicity question, Problem 2 is the parent of a class of problems we call Δ\Delta-d window start set. For integers n,ℓ,dn,\ell,d with ℓ|n\ell\mid n and d|ℓd\mid\ell, denote 𝒰n,ℓ↻⊆𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{U}^{\circlearrowright}_{n,\ell}\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell} to be the class of hypergraphs with hyperedges that are cyclic windows. Denote the hypergraph of Problem 2 as ℋn,ℓ↻\mathcal{H}^{\circlearrowright}_{n,\ell}, and its set of hypersdges ℱn,ℓ↻\mathcal{F}^{\circlearrowright}_{n,\ell}. Note that for each ℋd∈𝒰n,ℓ↻\mathcal{H}_{d}\in\mathcal{U}^{\circlearrowright}_{n,\ell} with hypersdges set ℱd⊆ℱn,ℓ↻\mathcal{F}_{d}\subseteq\mathcal{F}^{\circlearrowright}_{n,\ell} which is referred to as Δ\Delta-d start set, and the windows start positions are at distance dd apart. Note that ℋd∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{H}_{d}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell} is equivalent to ℋnd,ℓd↻∈𝒰nd,ℓd\mathcal{H}^{\circlearrowright}_{\frac{n}{d},\frac{\ell}{d}}\in\mathcal{U}_{\frac{n}{d},\frac{\ell}{d}}, which is the hypergraph of Problem 2 setting n′=n/dn^{\prime}=n/d and ℓ′=ℓ/d\ell^{\prime}=\ell/d (since there are nd\frac{n}{d} dd-lengthed blocks, and on each block start, a window starts, containing ℓd\frac{\ell}{d} blocks). As a consequence, proving the monotonicity for the Δ\Delta-d window class 𝒰↻n,ℓ\mathcal{U^{\circlearrowright}}_{n,\ell} is equivalent to proving the next lemma.11 1 one may ask why wasn’t the expression in Theorem 6 used in the proof. It is due to the complex nature of the inclusion-exclusion terms that makes it hard to compare.

Lemma 3.

For any n,ℓ,dn,\ell,d with d​∣ℓ∣​nd\mid\ell\mid n, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tnd,ℓd↻]≤𝔼⁡[Tn,ℓ↻].\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\circlearrowright}_{\,\frac{n}{d},\;\frac{\ell}{d}}\right]\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\circlearrowright}_{\,n,\;\ell}\right].

Equivalently, within the Δ\Delta-d family with fixed nn and ℓ\ell, making starts more discrete decreases the expected coverage time.

Proof:

The proof is a coupling argument, very similar to the proof of Lemma 2. Fix d​∣ℓ∣​nd\mid\ell\mid n and run the cyclic (n,ℓ)(n,\ell) model with starts uniformly on {0,1,…,n−1}\{0,1,\dots,n-1\} and windows winℓ↻​(i)\mathrm{win}^{\circlearrowright}_{\ell}(i). Define

ϕ⁡(i)=d⁡⌊id⌋∈{0,d,2​d,…,n−d},\phi(i)=d\Big\lfloor\tfrac{i}{d}\Big\rfloor\in\{0,d,2d,\dots,n-d\},

which is uniform over the Δ\Delta-d start set (each value has dd preimages), so using ϕ\phi gives a uniform Δ\Delta-d process (which justifies the coupling). In other words, the mapping shifts windows to start at multiples of dd (block starts). Let ℛ={w1,…,w|ℛ|}\mathcal{R}=\{w_{1},\dots,w_{|\mathcal{R}|}\} be the windows drawn up to Tn,ℓ↻T^{\circlearrowright}_{n,\ell} (they cover all nn positions). Consider any dd-block [j​d,(j+1)​d−1][jd,(j+1)d-1]. If it was covered by a window starting at j​djd, it remains covered after applying ϕ\phi. If not, some window in ℛ\mathcal{R} starts inside this block. So applying ϕ\phi moves the window start to position j​djd, covering the whole block. Thus all blocks are covered by the ϕ\phi-mapped sequence. Therefore, coverage in the cyclic windows model implies coverage in the Δ\Delta-d model. ∎

Remark 1.

The same coupling argument extends naturally to higher dimensions. For example, consider a 22-dimensional torus of size n1×n2n_{1}\times n_{2}, where each sample is a rectangular patch of ℓ1×ℓ2\ell_{1}\times\ell_{2}. If d1​∣ℓ1∣​n1d_{1}\mid\ell_{1}\mid n_{1} and d2​∣ℓ2∣​n2d_{2}\mid\ell_{2}\mid n_{2}, we can partition the torus into d1×d2d_{1}\times d_{2} blocks and define the mapping

ϕ⁡(i,j)=(d1​⌊i/d1⌋,d2​⌊j/d2⌋),\phi(i,j)=\big(d_{1}\lfloor i/d_{1}\rfloor,\;d_{2}\lfloor j/d_{2}\rfloor\big),

which is uniform over the Δ\Delta-(d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}) start set. The same block-covering argument shows that coverage in the full model implies coverage in the Δ\Delta-d model, yielding the same monotonicity property.

This monotonicity extends inductively to any dimension. Moreover, there is always a corresponding continuous version obtained by letting ni→∞n_{i}\to\infty while fixing the ratios ℓi/ni\ell_{i}/n_{i}, which dominates all discrete versions in expectation (by the same argument proving Lemma 2).

Remark 2.

For Problem 2, a lower bound of ⌊nℓ⌋​H⌊nℓ⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor H_{\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor} had been derived in the proof of Lemma 1. In the special case where ℓ|n\ell\mid n this mathces with a general lower bound that is true for all models, established in [26] for n=2n=2, and as stated in [28], can be extended to any ℓ|n\ell\mid n.

These monotonicity results suggest three universal principles which we believe are true.

Conjecture 1.

Given ℋ1,ℋ2∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{H}_{1},\mathcal{H}_{2}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, with the corresponding sets of hyperedges ℱ1,ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2} such that ℱ1⊆ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{2}, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tℋ1]≤𝔼⁡[Tℋ2].\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]\leq\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}_{2}}].
Conjecture 2.

Given ℋ∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tℋ]≤𝔼⁡[T([n]ℓ)].\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}]\leq\mathbb{E}[T_{\binom{[n]}{\ell}}].
Conjecture 3.

Given ℋ∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, it holds that

⌊nℓ⌋​H⌊nℓ⌋≤𝔼⁡[Tℋ].\lfloor\tfrac{n}{\ell}\rfloor H_{\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor}\leq\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}].

The conjectures suggest a universal upper bound on the uniform ℓ\ell-regular models. Furthermore, a conjecture by [27], later proved by [28], stated that the uniform distribution, corresponding to the batch coverage model in our terminology, does not achieve the minimal expected time. Our conjecture broadens the horizon of this idea and claims that not only is this model not optimal, but may even be the worst within the entire class 𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}.

Although the conjectures, and in particular Conjecture 2 remains currently unproved, a slightly weaker bound can already be established. The following theorem states this bound explicitly.

Theorem 10.

Given ℋ∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Tℋ]≤nℓ​(log⁡n+1).\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}]\;\leq\;\frac{n}{\ell}\,\big(\log n+1\big).
Proof:

Let UtU_{t} be the number of items not yet seen after tt draws. Due to uniformity, the probability for a position to not be sampled after tt rounds is (1−ℓn)t\big(1-\frac{\ell}{n}\big)^{t}. Thus, 𝔼⁡[Ut]=n​(1−ℓ/n)t\mathbb{E}[U_{t}]=n(1-\ell/n)^{t}. Using the tail-sum formula and Markov’s inequality, 𝔼[Tℋ]=∑r=1∞Pr[Tℋ≥r]=∑r=1∞Pr[Ur−1≥1]≤∑r=1t01+∑r=t0+1∞𝔼[Ur−1],\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}]=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\Pr[T_{\mathcal{H}}\geq r]=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\Pr[U_{r-1}\geq 1]\;\leq\;\sum_{r=1}^{t_{0}}1\;+\;\sum_{r=t_{0}+1}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}[U_{r-1}], where we choose t0:=⌈n​log⁡nℓ⌉t_{0}:=\left\lceil\tfrac{n\log n}{\ell}\right\rceil. Then ∑r=t0+1∞𝔼⁡[Ur−1]=n​∑r=t0∞(1−ℓ/n)r=n⋅(1−ℓ/n)t01−(1−ℓ/n)=n2ℓ​(1−ℓ/n)t0.\sum_{r=t_{0}+1}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}[U_{r-1}]=n\sum_{r=t_{0}}^{\infty}(1-\ell/n)^{r}=n\cdot\frac{(1-\ell/n)^{t_{0}}}{1-(1-\ell/n)}=\frac{n^{2}}{\ell}\,(1-\ell/n)^{t_{0}}. Using (1−ℓ/n)t0≤e−(ℓ/n)​t0≤e−(ℓ/n)⋅(nlogn/ℓ)=e−log⁡n=1/n(1-\ell/n)^{t_{0}}\leq e^{-(\ell/n)t_{0}}\leq e^{-(\ell/n)\cdot(n\log n/\ell)}=e^{-\log n}=1/n, we get

∑r=t0+1∞𝔼⁡[Ur−1]≤n2ℓ⋅1n=nℓ.\sum_{r=t_{0}+1}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}[U_{r-1}]\;\leq\;\frac{n^{2}}{\ell}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\;=\;\frac{n}{\ell}.

Therefore,

𝔼⁡[Tℋ]≤t0+nℓ≤nℓ​log⁡n+nℓ=nℓ​(log⁡n+1).\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathcal{H}}]\;\leq\;t_{0}+\frac{n}{\ell}\;\leq\;\frac{n}{\ell}\log n+\frac{n}{\ell}\;=\;\frac{n}{\ell}\,(\log n+1).

∎

VIII Future Work

A natural direction for future research is obtaining a more accurate asymptotic expression for the expectation in Problem 1. Unlike the cyclic or continuous versions, Problem 1 is harder to analyze, resulting in looser asymptotics which remain relatively crude.

Another important direction concerns the precision gap between the asymptotics of different models. For structured models such as the cyclic window (Problem 2), and its higher dimensional generalizations in 𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}, a lower bound of ⌊nℓ⌋​H⌊nℓ⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor H_{\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell}\rfloor} was established as mentioned in Remark 2, and is believed to be universal for 𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell} as stated in Conjecture 3. A universal upper bound of nℓ​(log⁡n+1)\frac{n}{\ell}(\log n+1) was established for 𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}.

The two bounds share the same leading term nℓ​log⁡n\tfrac{n}{\ell}\log n when ℓ=o⁡(n)\ell=o(n). On one hand, this is encouraging since it means that all such models are asymptotically solved. On the other hand, it highlights an important ambiguity: describing the expectation of a coverage problem as “asymptotically nℓ​log⁡n\tfrac{n}{\ell}\log n” is not very informative. Different models may yield the same asymptotic form, yet differ substantially in their non-leading terms.

Although the lower and upper bounds behave asymptotically the same with respect to the dominant term (in particular, their ratio approaches one as nn increases), there is an of O⁡(nℓ​log⁡ℓ)O(\frac{n}{\ell}\log\ell) gap in their difference. Closing this gap or analyzing the expectation for each model separately is left for future work. This suggests that further study of sub-leading terms and structural effects between models is essential to understand the fine behavior inside the regime where nℓ​log⁡(nℓ)≈nℓ​log⁡n\tfrac{n}{\ell}\log(\frac{n}{\ell})\approx\tfrac{n}{\ell}\log n.

Finally, proving or disproving either Conjecture 1 or Conjecture 2 could reveal deeper structural insights into coverage problems with uniform ℓ\ell-regular hypergraphs. Even a single counterexample or partial proof could illuminate the principles governing how geometry, overlap, and locality influence coverage time.
